reverseBrief.centralMentalModel: Different statistics measure different populations and questions; a frequency gap reflects conditions of access (tools, paid time, invitations) as much as individual choice, so it cannot be read as ability or interest.
reverseBrief.dailyLifeConnection: Two equally interested colleagues where only one gets an approved tool, paid learning time and an invitation to evaluate a process — and a manager staffing a pilot only from existing users.

explainBack.question: Why can't the Census finding that 30% of men versus 17% of women use AI daily be taken as evidence that women are less able or less interested in AI?
explainBack.answer: Because frequency of use reflects the conditions someone works under, not just her choices. If one worker is given an approved tool, paid time to practise and an invitation to evaluate a process, and another is simply told to keep up, the first will log more use regardless of relative ability or enthusiasm. The survey also only measured self-reported frequency among people who had already used AI for at least one task — it never asked about skill, interest, access, or whether daily use would even help each job. So the gap is compatible with unequal conditions and cannot identify a cause.
explainBack.expectedEvidence: A correct answer must distinguish what was measured (self-reported frequency among prior users, March 2026) from what was not (ability, interest, access, usefulness), and cite the conditions mechanism: tool provision, paid learning time and invitations drive usage independently of aptitude.
explainBack.assessment: The artifact fully supports this answer: P003 defines the measured population, P004 lists what the figures do not measure, and P006 supplies the causal conditions mechanism with its explicit limit.

unseenTransfer.scenario: A hospital reports that nurses on day shifts file 3x more AI-assisted patient notes than night-shift nurses, and administrators propose recruiting the AI documentation steering committee from the highest-volume users. Day shifts have on-site IT support and scheduled training hours; night shifts have neither.
unseenTransfer.question: Using the article's mechanism, what does the 3x usage gap show, and what is wrong with staffing the committee from the highest-volume users?
unseenTransfer.answer: The usage gap measures conditions, not aptitude: day-shift nurses have supported access (IT help, scheduled training time), so higher volume tells us little about night nurses' ability or interest. Selecting the committee from existing heavy users repeats the P007 selection error — people who never had supported access lose the next opportunity too, so the gap compounds. The hospital should instead examine how it distributes training time and support across shifts, and open committee selection beyond current users; rising login counts alone would not show the decisions became fairer.
unseenTransfer.expectedEvidence: Application of two article moves: (1) frequency reflects access conditions, not ability (P004, P006); (2) selecting participants from existing users compounds the access gap, and usage metrics cannot verify fairness (P007).
unseenTransfer.assessment: The article's mechanism transfers cleanly to this unseen case: both the measurement critique and the compounding-selection step apply without modification, confirming the explanation generalizes.
